claim: Rhythmic activity in the theta range is thought to promote neuronal communication between brain regions.
source: Rhythmic activity in the theta range is thought to promote neuronal communication between brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific understanding about theta rhythms.

claim: Social encounters were associated with increased rhythmicity in the high theta range (7–10 Hz).
source: Social encounters were associated with increased rhythmicity in the high theta range (7–10 Hz) that was proportional to the stimulus degree of novelty.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The modulation of theta rhythmicity during social encounters was proportional to the stimulus degree of novelty.
source: Social encounters were associated with increased rhythmicity in the high theta range (7–10 Hz) that was proportional to the stimulus degree of novelty.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data showing changes across encounters.

claim: The modulation of theta rhythmicity was specific for social stimuli.
source: This modulation of theta rhythmicity, which was specific for social stimuli, appeared to reflect a brain-state of social arousal.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparisons with object stimuli in the results.

claim: The same network responded to a fearful stimulus by enhancement of rhythmicity in the low theta range (3–7 Hz).
source: In contrast, the same network responded to a fearful stimulus by enhancement of rhythmicity in the low theta range (3–7 Hz).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fear conditioning experiments.

claim: Theta rhythmicity showed different patterns of coherence between distinct brain regions in response to social and fearful stimuli.
source: Moreover, theta rhythmicity showed different pattern of coherence between the distinct brain regions in response to social and fearful stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by coherence analyses in the results section.

claim: The two types of stimuli induce distinct arousal states that elicit different patterns of theta rhythmicity.
source: We suggest that the two types of stimuli induce distinct arousal states that elicit different patterns of theta rhythmicity, which cause the same brain areas to communicate in different modes.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings presented.

claim: Oscillatory brain activity is thought to coordinate neural activity in vast neuronal assemblies dispersed over different brain regions.
source: Oscillatory brain activity, mostly categorized to the theta (3–12 Hz), beta (12–30 Hz), and gamma (30–80 Hz) bands, is thought to coordinate neural activity in vast neuronal assemblies dispersed over different brain regions (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Oscillatory brain activity may underlie high level cognitive functions, such as speech and social communication.
source: This type of coordination may underlie high level cognitive functions, such as speech and social communication (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2006; Uhlhaas et al., 2009) that are impaired in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) (Geschwind, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individuals with ASD show deficits in long-range neuronal communication associated with low-frequency rhythms, such as the theta rhythm.
source: Increasing evidence suggest that individuals with ASD show deficits in long-range neuronal communication associated with low-frequency rhythms, such as the theta rhythm (Geschwind and Levitt, 2007; Rippon et al., 2007; Wass, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A clear connection between rhythmic brain activity and social behavior has not yet been established.
source: Nonetheless, a clear connection between rhythmic brain activity and social behavior has not yet been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Mammalian social organization depends on the ability to recognize and remember individual conspecifics.
source: Mammalian social organization depends on the ability to recognize and remember individual conspecifics (Wiley, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Social recognition memory can be assessed in rodents using their innate tendency to investigate novel conspecifics more persistently than familiar ones.
source: This social recognition memory (SRM) can be assessed in rodents using their innate tendency to investigate novel conspecifics more persistently than familiar ones (Gheusi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the SRM habituation–dishabituation test, social memory is assessed by the gradual reduction in the amount of time the animal spends investigating a particular social stimulus during consecutive encounters.
source: In the SRM habituation–dishabituation test, social memory is assessed by the gradual reduction in the amount of time the animal spends investigating a particular social stimulus during consecutive encounters (Ferguson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the behavioral paradigm.

claim: Short-term social memory was shown to be mediated mainly by chemical cues (semiochemicals) perceived via the main and accessory olfactory systems.
source: This short-term memory was shown to be mediated mainly by chemical cues (semiochemicals) perceived via the main and accessory olfactory systems (Dulac and Torello, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Upon binding of semiochemicals to receptors, sensory information is conveyed to the main (MOB) and accessory (AOB) olfactory bulbs.
source: Upon binding of semiochemicals to the receptors expressed by the sensory neurons of the main olfactory epithelium and the vomeronasal organ, sensory information is conveyed to the main (MOB) and accessory (AOB) olfactory bulbs, respectively (Dulac and Wagner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the neural pathway.

claim: Both MOB and AOB project, directly and indirectly, to the medial amygdala (MeA).
source: Both bulbs then project, directly and indirectly, to the medial amygdala (MeA) (Pro-Sistiaga et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2011) that is thought to transfer the information to the hippocampus through the lateral septum (LS) (Bielsky and Young, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing neural connectivity.

claim: The MeA is thought to transfer information to the hippocampus through the lateral septum (LS).
source: Both bulbs then project, directly and indirectly, to the medial amygdala (MeA) (Pro-Sistiaga et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2011) that is thought to transfer the information to the hippocampus through the lateral septum (LS) (Bielsky and Young, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the neural pathway.

claim: The MOB projects to several cortical areas comprising the primary olfactory cortex, of which the piriform cortex (Pir) is best characterized.
source: The MOB projects also to several cortical areas comprising the primary olfactory cortex, of which the piriform cortex (Pir) is best characterized (Wilson and Sullivan, 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A highly rhythmic LFP was recorded in all brain areas during social encounters.
source: A highly rhythmic LFP was recorded in all brain areas during social encounters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Power spectral density (PSD) analysis of the LFP showed a prominent peak at ∼8 Hz, typical for the high theta band, in all areas.
source: Power spectral density (PSD) analysis of the LFP showed a prominent peak at ∼8 Hz, typical for the high theta band (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004), in all areas (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 2C, with citation for theta band classification.

claim: Theta power was very low in the absence of a social stimulus but increased profoundly during the first encounter.
source: The value of this peak, termed theta power (TP), was very low in the absence of a social stimulus (Base, Figure 2D–E) but increased profoundly during the first encounter (Enc. 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figures 2D-E.

claim: Theta power gradually decreased during further encounters with the same stimulus but increased again when another novel stimulus was introduced.
source: It then gradually decreased during further encounters with the same stimulus (Enc. 2–4), but increased again when another novel stimulus was introduced (Enc. 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Changes in theta power during SRM testing closely followed the changes in investigation time.
source: These changes in theta power during SRM testing closely followed the changes in investigation time (IT) (Figure 2F), with both parameters appearing to correlate with the degree of stimulus novelty.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both theta power and investigation time appear to correlate with the degree of stimulus novelty.
source: These changes in theta power during SRM testing closely followed the changes in investigation time (IT) (Figure 2F), with both parameters appearing to correlate with the degree of stimulus novelty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Exposure of an animal to either social or non-social stimuli caused similar dynamics of the investigation time.
source: As exemplified in Figure 3A (lower panel), exposure of an animal to either type of stimulus caused similar dynamics of the investigation time.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a vast difference in theta power response to social and non-social stimuli.
source: However, there was a vast difference with regards to the theta power response to the social and non-social stimuli: whereas significant theta power modulation that was similar across all brain regions was observed with social stimuli, whether awake or anesthetized, object and odor stimuli did not cause such an effect (Figure 3A, upper panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Significant theta power modulation was observed with social stimuli, whether awake or anesthetized.
source: However, there was a vast difference with regards to the theta power response to the social and non-social stimuli: whereas significant theta power modulation that was similar across all brain regions was observed with social stimuli, whether awake or anesthetized, object and odor stimuli did not cause such an effect (Figure 3A, upper panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Object and odor stimuli did not cause theta power modulation.
source: However, there was a vast difference with regards to the theta power response to the social and non-social stimuli: whereas significant theta power modulation that was similar across all brain regions was observed with social stimuli, whether awake or anesthetized, object and odor stimuli did not cause such an effect (Figure 3A, upper panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Social stimuli caused a marked increase of mean theta power during Enc. 1 compared to Base, with the MOB and AOB showing the largest changes (6.2 dB/Hz) and other areas showing more moderate ones (4.0–5.1 dB/Hz).
source: Social stimuli caused a marked increase of mean theta power during Enc. 1 compared to Base, with the MOB and AOB showing the largest changes (6.2 dB/Hz) and other areas showing more moderate ones (4.0–5.1 dB/Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: In all regions tested, the theta power decreased gradually during the habituation phase (Enc. 1–4) but returned to the values obtained in Enc. 1 after dishabituation (Enc. 5).
source: In all regions tested, the theta power decreased gradually during the habituation phase (Enc. 1–4) but returned the values obtained in Enc. 1 after dishabituation (Enc. 5) (p < 0.005 one-way repeated measures ANOVA, *pcorr < 0.05 post-hoc paired t-test, Figure 3—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is a statistically significant observation from the experimental data.

claim: Object stimuli elicited a much weaker initial change from Base to Enc. 1 (1.1–2.7 dB/Hz) in all brain regions compared to social stimuli.
source: In contrast, object stimuli elicited a much weaker initial change from Base to Enc. 1 (1.1–2.7 dB/Hz) in all brain regions.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: The theta power showed modulation during the object paradigm similarly to the social paradigm only in the MOB, and even this change was not statistically significant.
source: Furthermore, the theta power showed modulation during the object paradigm similarly to the social paradigm only in the MOB, and even this change was not statistically significant (p > 0.05, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the experimental data.

claim: Comparison of the investigation time of the social and object paradigms showed a highly similar course and magnitude of habituation and dishabituation that were statistically significant in both cases.
source: In a sharp contrast to the theta power, comparison of the investigation time of the social and object paradigms showed a highly similar course and magnitude of habituation and dishabituation that were statistically significant in both cases (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In almost all recorded brain areas, theta power is modulated by the degree of novelty of social but not object stimuli.
source: Taken together, these results show that in almost all recorded brain areas, theta power is modulated by the degree of novelty of social but not object stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The lack of theta power modulation despite clear investigation time modulation induced by object stimuli rejects the possibility that theta rhythmicity is caused by investigative behavior.
source: The lack of theta power modulation despite the clear investigation time modulation induced by object stimuli rejects the possibility that the theta rhythmicity is caused by the investigative behavior.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Theta rhythmicity did not cease with the removal of the social stimulus following Enc. 1, but remained at a high level during most of the Post 1 period.
source: As depicted in Figure 4A, the theta rhythmicity did not cease with the removal of the social stimulus following Enc. 1, but remained at a high level during most of the Post 1 period (for spectrograms of the full experiment, see Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All encounters with a social stimulus were followed by sustained high theta power during the Post period.
source: Plotting the mean instantaneous theta power as a function of time, revealed that this was true for all encounters with a social stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Encounters with object stimuli were followed by a sharp drop in theta power to a low level almost immediately following stimulus removal.
source: In contrast, encounters with object stimuli were followed by a sharp drop in the theta power to a low level almost immediately following stimulus removal (Figure 4B, for all other brain areas see Figure 4—figure supplements 6–7).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a significant reduction in mean theta power between the Enc. and Post periods of the object paradigm in all brain areas.
source: This significant reduction in mean theta power between the Enc. and Post periods of the object paradigm was characteristic of all brain areas (Figure 4C, *p < 0.05 paired t-test, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High theta power levels were found in both Enc. and Post periods in the social paradigm.
source: In contrast, high theta power levels were found in both these periods in the social paradigm (p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the experimental data.

claim: All encounters with social stimuli showed a steep but gradual increase in theta power during the first 15 s in which the stimulus was being transferred into the arena.
source: Moreover, all encounters with social stimuli showed a steep but gradual increase in theta power during the first 15 s in which the stimulus was being transferred into the arena (Figure 4A,D, gray bars).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 4A and 4D.

claim: The rise in theta power during stimulus transfer probably reflects the subject's anticipation for a social meeting.
source: This rise in theta power probably reflects the subject's anticipation for a social meeting, as there was no similar increase with object stimuli (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of social and object stimuli data.

claim: The changes in theta power during the SRM test reflect a graded internal brain state of arousal that is proportional to the novelty of the social stimulus and slowly fades away after its removal.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the changes in theta power during the SRM test reflect a graded internal brain state of arousal that is proportional to the novelty of the social stimulus and slowly fades away after its removal.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Despite the fact that both MOB and AOB are directly connected to the MeA, the strongest correlation appeared with the LS and the weakest with the MOB.
source: Despite the fact that both areas are directly connected to the MeA, the strongest correlation appeared with the LS and the weakest with the MOB (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: The correlation between the MeA and LS was significantly higher during Enc. 1 compared to Base.
source: Moreover, whereas the correlation between the MeA and LS was significantly higher during Enc. 1 (blue) compared to Base (red), the MOB showed consistently low correlation with the MeA during both periods.
evidence: This is an observation from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The MOB showed consistently low correlation with the MeA during both Base and Enc. 1 periods.
source: Moreover, whereas the correlation between the MeA and LS was significantly higher during Enc. 1 (blue) compared to Base (red), the MOB showed consistently low correlation with the MeA during both periods.
evidence: This is an observation from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The presence of a social stimulus differentially affects the correlation of theta rhythmicity between distinct brain areas.
source: The presence of a social stimulus thus appears to differentially affect the correlation of theta rhythmicity between distinct brain areas.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the cross-correlation data.

claim: The coherence between the MeA and the LS showed several prominent peaks, especially in the theta and gamma bands.
source: As depicted in Figure 6A, the coherence between the MeA and the LS showed several prominent peaks, especially in the theta and gamma bands.
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: While no change was recorded in the gamma band, the theta coherence showed a significant increase between the Base and Enc. 1.
source: Yet, while no change was recorded in the gamma band, the theta coherence showed a significant increase between the Base and Enc. 1.
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: The high coherence at theta range between MeA and LS persisted during the Post 1 period despite the lack of a social stimulus.
source: Furthermore, similarly to theta rhythmicity itself (Figure 4), the high coherence at theta range persisted during the Post 1 period despite the lack of a social stimulus (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: The coherence in theta band between the MeA and MOB remained low throughout all periods.
source: In contrast, the coherence in theta band between the MeA and MOB remained low throughout all periods (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: There is a hierarchy in the theta coherence between the MeA and all other areas, ranging from a low level with the MOB and AOB, medium coherence with the Pir and high coherence with the LS.
source: Analyses across all regions revealed a hierarchy in the theta coherence between the MeA and all other areas, ranging from a low level with the MOB and AOB, medium coherence with the Pir and high coherence with the LS (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Despite their largest physical distance, the highest level of theta coherence was found between the MeAs in the two hemispheres.
source: This notion of functional hierarchy between brain regions is strengthened by the fact that despite their largest physical distance, the highest level of theta coherence was found between the MeAs in the two hemispheres (Figure 6—figure supplements 1,3).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figure 6 supplements.

claim: The theta coherence between the MeA and the higher brain centers (Pir, LS) significantly increased during Enc. 1 and Post 1.
source: Furthermore, the theta coherence between the MeA and the higher brain centers (Pir, LS) significantly increased during Enc. 1 and Post 1 (*pcorr < 0.05, paired t-test, Figure 6—source data 1), while no change was recorded between the MeA and both areas of the olfactory bulb (MOB, AOB, pcorr > 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: No change in theta coherence was recorded between the MeA and both areas of the olfactory bulb (MOB, AOB) during social encounters.
source: Furthermore, the theta coherence between the MeA and the higher brain centers (Pir, LS) significantly increased during Enc. 1 and Post 1 (*pcorr < 0.05, paired t-test, Figure 6—source data 1), while no change was recorded between the MeA and both areas of the olfactory bulb (MOB, AOB, pcorr > 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: There exist at least two independent theta rhythms, one that governs the olfactory bulb and another that dominates higher brain structures.
source: This suggests the existence of at least two independent theta rhythms, one that governs the olfactory bulb and another that dominates higher brain structures.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the coherence data.

claim: The MOB shows opposite relationships with all other brain areas; high coherence with the AOB and low coherence with the higher areas.
source: This conclusion is further supported by the findings that the MOB shows opposite relationships with all other brain areas; high coherence with the AOB and low coherence with the higher areas (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figure 6E and supplements.

claim: A significant enhancement in theta coherence between MOB and AOB was observed during Enc. 1 and Post1.
source: Moreover, a significant enhancement in theta coherence with the AOB was observed during Enc. 1 and Post1 (*pcorr < 0.05, paired t-test, Figure 6—source data 1), while all other regions showed no change (pcorr > 0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: Similar enhancement of theta coherence between the AOB and MOB was recorded with object stimuli.
source: Interestingly, similar enhancement of theta coherence between the AOB and MOB was recorded with object stimuli, while these stimuli did not cause any enhancement of the coherence between the MeA and LS or Pir (Figure 6F,G, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Object stimuli did not cause any enhancement of the coherence between the MeA and LS or Pir.
source: Interestingly, similar enhancement of theta coherence between the AOB and MOB was recorded with object stimuli, while these stimuli did not cause any enhancement of the coherence between the MeA and LS or Pir (Figure 6F,G, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Theta rhythmicity was previously found to be elicited in several brain regions during states of arousal, mainly in response to fearful stimuli.
source: Theta rhythmicity was previously found to be elicited in several brain regions during states of arousal, mainly in response to fearful stimuli (Knyazev, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A recall of a fearful memory, induced by a fear-conditioned stimulus, elicits robust theta rhythmicity that shows high coherence between brain regions in the fear network.
source: In this network, a recall of a fearful memory, induced by a fear-conditioned stimulus, elicits robust theta rhythmicity that shows high coherence between these brain regions (Paré and Collins, 2000; Pare et al., 2002; Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Pape et al., 2005; Popa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Introduction of the fear-conditioned tone caused animals to begin moving intensively, followed by immobility (freezing) towards the end of the tone.
source: During the FC experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), introduction of the fear-conditioned tone caused animals to begin moving intensively, followed by immobility (freezing) towards the end of the tone, in anticipation of the foot shock.
evidence: This is an observation from the fear conditioning experiments shown in Figure 7 supplement 1B.

claim: The freezing response was especially significant at the end of the first tone.
source: The freezing response was especially significant at the end of the first tone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7 supplement 1C.

claim: The fear-conditioned tone caused a robust arousal state that was associated with intense movement of the conditioned animals.
source: Thus, the fear-conditioned tone caused a robust arousal state that was associated with intense movement of the conditioned animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral observations.

claim: The fear stimulus caused a marked peak at the low theta range (3–7 Hz), while the social stimulus resulted in a peak at the high theta range (7–10 Hz).
source: Whereas the fear stimulus caused a marked peak at the low theta range (3–7 Hz), the social stimulus resulted in a peak at the high theta range (7–10 Hz).
evidence: This is an observation from the PSD analysis comparing fear and social stimuli.

claim: The differences in theta range between fear and social stimuli appeared in all recorded brain regions.
source: This change is clearly observed when subtracting the Base PSD from the Stimulus profile (Figure 7B). These differences appeared in all recorded brain regions (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Statistical analysis showed a highly significant interaction between the type of experiment (FC or SR) and theta band.
source: Statistical analysis showed a highly significant interaction between the type of experiment (FC or SR) and theta band (Figure 7D) (**p < 0.01, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Fearful and social stimuli cause changes in very different ranges of theta rhythmicity in the same limbic network of brain regions.
source: Thus, we conclude that fearful and social stimuli cause changes in very different ranges of theta rhythmicity in the same limbic network of brain regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing fear and social stimuli.

claim: The low theta reflects aversive arousal that is associated with fear while the high theta reflects appetitive arousal associated with a social encounter.
source: We suggest that these different types of theta rhythmicity reflect distinct arousal states; the low theta reflects aversive arousal that is associated with fear while the high theta reflects appetitive arousal associated with a social encounter.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The magnitude of coherence changes was different between distinct pairs of brain regions.
source: Nevertheless, the magnitude of changes was different between distinct pairs.
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: The increases of coherence between the AOB-MOB and MOB-Pir pairs were much bigger in SR compared to the FC experiment.
source: Moreover, the increases of coherence between the AOB-MOB and MOB-Pir pairs were much bigger in SR compared to the FC experiment.
evidence: This is an observation from the coherence analysis.

claim: The distinct arousal states are characterized by distinct patterns of coherence changes within the same network of brain regions.
source: We conclude that the distinct arousal states are characterized by distinct patterns of coherence changes within that same network of brain regions (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coherence analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: An encounter with a social stimulus causes increased LFP rhythmicity in the high theta range (7–10 Hz), in a network of limbic brain areas associated with social memory.
source: This study demonstrates that an encounter with a social stimulus causes increased LFP rhythmicity in the high theta range (7–10 Hz), in a network of limbic brain areas associated with social memory.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: The change in theta rhythmicity is directly proportional to the novelty of the social partner.
source: Strikingly, the change in theta rhythmicity is directly proportional to the novelty of the social partner, and may thus be considered a neuronal correlate of short-term social memory (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data, with a citation to related work.

claim: The change in theta rhythmicity may be considered a neuronal correlate of short-term social memory.
source: Strikingly, the change in theta rhythmicity is directly proportional to the novelty of the social partner, and may thus be considered a neuronal correlate of short-term social memory (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion with a citation to related work.

claim: The modulation of theta rhythmicity does not depend on the behavior of the social stimulus since it is observed even when anesthetized stimuli are used.
source: Since the modulation of theta rhythmicity is observed even when anesthetized stimuli are used, we infer that it does not depend on the behavior of the social stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation with anesthetized stimuli.

claim: The modulation of theta rhythmicity is social specific since it is not observed with object stimuli despite similarity in investigative behavior.
source: Despite the similarity in investigative behavior, such modulation of theta rhythmicity is not observed with object stimuli, suggesting that it is social specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of social and object stimuli.

claim: The augmented theta rhythmicity and the associated increase in theta coherence persist beyond the removal of the social stimulus itself.
source: Since the augmented theta rhythmicity and the associated increase in theta coherence persist beyond the removal of the social stimulus itself, we conclude that these parameters do not mirror sensory inputs but rather reflect a state of arousal that slowly fades away.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Theta rhythmicity and coherence do not mirror sensory inputs but rather reflect a state of arousal that slowly fades away.
source: Since the augmented theta rhythmicity and the associated increase in theta coherence persist beyond the removal of the social stimulus itself, we conclude that these parameters do not mirror sensory inputs but rather reflect a state of arousal that slowly fades away.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the persistence of theta activity after stimulus removal.

claim: The increase in theta power occurs prior to the actual introduction of the social stimulus in the arena, suggesting increased arousal due to the anticipated social encounter.
source: This is in agreement with the fact that the increase in theta power occurs prior to the actual introduction of the social stimulus in the arena, suggesting increased arousal due to the anticipated social encounter.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that theta power increases during stimulus transfer.

claim: The change in theta rhythmicity during the SRM test reflects a graded level of arousal, which is proportional to the stimulus saliency.
source: Finally, since the change in theta rhythmicity during the SRM test correlates with the novelty of the social stimulus, we posit that it reflects a graded level of arousal, which is proportional to the stimulus saliency.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the correlation between theta power and stimulus novelty.

claim: The social stimulus is much more complex than the single object or odor stimuli used as controls.
source: Notably, the social stimulus is much more complex than the single object or odor stimuli that we used as controls.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The social stimulus emits a complex mixture of odors and semiochemicals, and stimulates the visual, auditory, and somatosensory systems in addition to the main and accessory olfactory systems.
source: It emits a complex mixture of odors and semiochemicals, and in addition to the main and accessory olfactory systems, it also stimulates the visual, auditory, and somatosensory systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of social stimuli.

claim: It is not likely that the full complexity of the social stimulus may be mimicked by the use of any artificial mixture of odors.
source: It is not likely that the full complexity of the social stimulus may be mimicked by the use of any artificial mixture of odors, hence the possibility that the arousal state results from the complexity of the stimulus cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a limitation of the study.

claim: A very simple cue is sufficient to evoke a state of arousal in fear-associated contexts, such as freezing of rodents in response to TMT or a pure tone in fear conditioning.
source: On the other hand, at least as regards to fear-associated arousal, it is well documented (Takahashi et al., 2008) that a very simple cue is sufficient to evoke a state of arousal, such that is observed by the freezing of rodents in response to the pure odorant 2,3,5-Trimethyl-3-thiazoline (TMT), a component of fox odor (Fendt et al., 2003), or to a pure tone in a fear conditioning paradigm (Rogan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on fear conditioning.

claim: The factor that determines the state of arousal is not the complexity of the stimulus but rather the information it embodies with regards to the natural environment of the animal.
source: This suggests that the factor that determines the state of arousal is not the complexity of the stimulus but rather the information it embodies with regards to the natural environment of the animal.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the comparison of simple and complex arousing stimuli.

claim: Many studies, both in animals and humans, have linked brain theta rhythmicity to the processing of emotional cues.
source: Many studies, both in animals and humans, have linked brain theta rhythmicity to the processing of emotional cues (Sainsbury and Montoya, 1984; Sainsbury et al., 1987a; Sainsbury et al., 1987b; Aftanas et al., 2001; Balconi and Pozzoli, 2009; Knyazev et al., 2009; Maratos et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In animals, theta rhythmicity was mostly studied in the hippocampus where it was classified into two types, Type 1 and Type 2.
